competency_fulfillment.rationale: The two describing clauses land squarely. "Counting up" is literal in seed 46, "Start at 12. Count up 7 more. What number do you land on?", and in seed 603, "Start at 4. Count up 3 more. You land on ___". "Putting together" is literal in seed 45, "One group has 4 items and another group has 13 items. If you put them together, how many items are there in all?", and seed 47, "One group has 1 item and another group has 10 items. Putting them together makes ___ items in all." But the lead verb is to "Illustrate" using models, and most items illustrate nothing — seed 52 is purely abstract part-whole language, "The two parts are 1 and 7. What is the sum?", with no model, no objects and no picture.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Two of the three clauses are covered well, but "a variety of concrete and pictorial models" is served by only three of 18 samples: seed 43's star array ("There are 18 stars." then "1 more star is added."), seed 500's cup array ("There are 12 drinks."), and seed 66's "Show 12 + 7 on the number line." Those two emoji items are the same model with a different icon, so the stated "variety" reduces to one pictorial type plus one number line. No concrete model (counters, blocks, fingers, ten-frame) appears anywhere; the closest is the generic noun in seed 600, "One group has 11 items and another group has 7 items."

cognitive_capacity.rationale: This is Grade 1 Quarter 1, the first quarter of formal schooling, yet the dominant stem is a long text-only sentence with no picture to lean on: seed 501 reads "One group has 15 items and another group has 2 items. Putting them together makes 17 items in all. True or False?" — 19 words and two embedded numbers for an emergent reader, with the word "items" carrying no concrete referent. Seed 52's "The two parts are 1 and 7. What is the sum?" asks for abstract part-whole vocabulary at the point in the year when the competency expects models. The genuinely age-fitted items are the picture ones, seeds 43 and 500, and they are the minority.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Two templates account for 14 of 18 samples: the group-combining sentence (seeds 44, 45, 47, 68, 501, 502, 600) and the count-up sentence (seeds 42, 46, 601, 603, 604, 606, 607), each repeated near-verbatim with only the numerals changed — compare seed 601, "Start at 10. Count up 5 more. What number do you land on?", with seed 607, "Start at 10. Count up 9 more. What number do you land on?". Operands repeat as well: 12 and 7 drive three separate items (seed 46's count-up, seed 66's "Show 12 + 7 on the number line.", and seed 500's drinks picture), and six items land on the answer 19. The noun is "items" in every group item; no real objects vary.

competency_alignment.rationale: Nothing exceeds Grade 1 Quarter 1. Every operation is addition, every sum is at or under 20 (seed 44's 10 + 10 = 20 is the ceiling), and the only technical words used are ones the competency itself sanctions — "counting up" language in seed 606, "Start at 18. Count up 1 more. What number do you land on?", and putting-together language in seed 68, "One group has 13 items and another group has 1 item. Putting them together makes 14 items in all. True or False?" No subtraction, no place-value naming, no regrouping vocabulary appears.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: All sums fall inside "sums up to 20": the largest is seed 44's 20 ("One group has 10 items and another group has 10 items."), and the smallest, seed 42's start at 4 counting up 2 to 6, gives an appropriate low anchor. Addends span 1 to 18 (seed 43's 18 stars plus 1; seed 52's "The two parts are 1 and 7."), so both the small-number and near-ceiling ends of the band are exercised. Distractors above 20, such as 29 at seed 46 and 30 at seed 44, are lures only and are never presented as sums.
